questions.stem: What are the three components that make up total storage cost in Snowflake?

options.text: Compute credits, staged file storage, and database table storage
Staged file storage, database table storage, and Fail-safe/Time Travel storage
Active storage, query cache storage, and metadata storage
Internal stage storage, external stage storage, and table storage

explanation.correct: Total storage cost is the sum of staged file storage, database table storage, and Fail-safe and Time Travel storage.

distractors.A: Compute credits are a separate cost category from storage.
distractors.C: Query cache and metadata are not billed as storage components.
distractors.D: External stages are not Snowflake-managed storage; storage cost refers to staged files, tables, and CDP data.

questions.stem: Which view provides the most detailed breakdown of physical storage for table data across Active, Time Travel, and Fail-safe states?

options.text: DATABASE_STORAGE_USAGE_HISTORY
STAGE_STORAGE_USAGE_HISTORY
TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS
STORAGE_DAILY_HISTORY

explanation.correct: TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS provides the most detailed information with columns for ACTIVE_BYTES, TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES, and FAILSAFE_BYTES, plus clone-related storage columns.

distractors.A: DATABASE_STORAGE_USAGE_HISTORY shows daily storage at the database level, not per-table breakdown by CDP state.
distractors.B: STAGE_STORAGE_USAGE_HISTORY covers stage storage, not table CDP lifecycle storage.
distractors.D: STORAGE_DAILY_HISTORY combines database and stage storage at an aggregate level.

questions.stem: What is the maximum Time Travel retention period for a transient table?

options.text: 7 days
90 days
0 or 1 day
30 days

explanation.correct: Transient tables (and temporary tables) can have a Time Travel retention period of only 0 or 1 day, and they have no Fail-safe.

distractors.A: 7 days is the Fail-safe period for permanent tables, not the Time Travel for transient tables.
distractors.B: 90 days is the maximum Time Travel for permanent tables on Enterprise Edition.
distractors.D: 30 days is not applicable to transient tables.

questions.stem: Which THREE columns in the TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS view represent the CDP lifecycle storage states? (Select THREE)

options.text: ACTIVE_BYTES
RETAINED_FOR_CLONE_BYTES
TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES
FAILSAFE_BYTES
STAGED_BYTES
COMPRESSED_BYTES

explanation.correct: ACTIVE_BYTES, TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES, and FAILSAFE_BYTES represent the three sequential CDP lifecycle states in the TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS view.

distractors.B: RETAINED_FOR_CLONE_BYTES tracks storage retained for cloned tables, not a CDP lifecycle state.
distractors.E: STAGED_BYTES is not a column in TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS.
distractors.F: COMPRESSED_BYTES is not a column in TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about staged file storage in Snowflake are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: Staged files are subject to Time Travel and Fail-safe storage costs
Staged files incur standard data storage costs only
Files should be removed from stages after loading to manage costs
External stage files are charged as Snowflake storage
Staged files are automatically purged after 30 days

explanation.correct: Data files in internal stages incur standard storage costs but are NOT subject to Time Travel or Fail-safe. Snowflake recommends removing files after loading to manage costs.

distractors.A: Staged files are NOT subject to Time Travel or Fail-safe costs.
distractors.D: External stage files are stored outside Snowflake and charged by the cloud provider, not Snowflake.
distractors.E: Staged files are not automatically purged; they must be manually removed or removed during loading.

questions.scenario: A company has a permanent table on Enterprise Edition with DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS set to 30.
questions.stem: What is the maximum number of days that historical data is maintained for this table?

options.text: 30 days
37 days
38 days
7 days

explanation.correct: On Enterprise Edition, a permanent table with 30 days Time Travel plus 7 days Fail-safe = 37 days maximum historical data maintained.

distractors.A: 30 days is only the Time Travel period; Fail-safe adds 7 more days.
distractors.C: 38 would imply 31 days of Time Travel or 8 days of Fail-safe, neither of which is correct.
distractors.D: 7 days is the Fail-safe period alone, not the total.

questions.scenario: A data engineer clones a 500 GB table. Immediately after cloning, no modifications have been made to either table.
questions.stem: How much additional storage does the cloned table consume?

options.text: 500 GB (a full copy)
250 GB (half the original)
No additional storage until changes are made to the clone
A small metadata overhead of approximately 1 MB

explanation.correct: Zero-copy cloning means the clone initially shares all existing micro-partitions with the original table. No additional storage is consumed until rows are added, updated, or deleted in the clone.

distractors.A: A clone does not create a full copy of the data; it shares micro-partitions.
distractors.B: There is no partial copy; storage is shared entirely until changes are made.
distractors.D: While there is minimal metadata, the key point is no data storage cost, not a specific 1 MB overhead.

questions.scenario: An administrator notices that TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES and FAILSAFE_BYTES increase immediately after loading data via COPY INTO, even though no rows were updated or deleted.
questions.stem: What causes this behavior?

options.text: COPY INTO always creates a full backup of the table before loading
Small micro-partition defragmentation during loading deletes small micro-partitions and creates new ones
Time Travel is triggered by any new transaction, including inserts
The staging area files are counted toward TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES

explanation.correct: During data loading (INSERT, COPY, SNOWPIPE), small micro-partition defragmentation deletes small micro-partitions and creates new consolidated ones. The deleted micro-partitions contribute to TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES and FAILSAFE_BYTES.

distractors.A: COPY INTO does not create a full backup; it adds data which may trigger defragmentation.
distractors.C: Pure inserts into new micro-partitions do not inherently generate Time Travel bytes; it's the defragmentation of small partitions that causes it.
distractors.D: Staging area files are not counted in TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES.

questions.stem: Which TWO approaches help identify high-churn tables? (Select TWO)

options.text: Calculate the ratio of FAILSAFE_BYTES to ACTIVE_BYTES in TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS
Check the QUERY_HISTORY view for tables with the most UPDATE statements
Look for tables where FAILSAFE_BYTES is significantly larger than ACTIVE_BYTES
Monitor the AUTO_CLUSTERING_HISTORY for excessive reclustering
Check the TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES column for tables with zero bytes

explanation.correct: High-churn tables are identified by calculating the ratio of FAILSAFE_BYTES divided by ACTIVE_BYTES. A large ratio indicates high churn where historical data far exceeds active data.

distractors.B: QUERY_HISTORY shows query activity but doesn't directly reveal CDP storage impact ratios.
distractors.D: AUTO_CLUSTERING_HISTORY relates to clustering maintenance, not CDP churn identification.
distractors.E: Zero TIME_TRAVEL_BYTES would indicate no recent changes, the opposite of high churn.

questions.scenario: A company wants to view storage costs in their local currency rather than in bytes.
questions.stem: Which view converts storage size into cost in currency?

options.text: DATABASE_STORAGE_USAGE_HISTORY
TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS
STORAGE_DAILY_HISTORY
USAGE_IN_CURRENCY_DAILY

explanation.correct: The USAGE_IN_CURRENCY_DAILY view in ORGANIZATION_USAGE converts the size of storage into cost in currency using the daily price of a TB.

distractors.A: DATABASE_STORAGE_USAGE_HISTORY reports storage in bytes, not currency.
distractors.B: TABLE_STORAGE_METRICS reports bytes per table, not currency values.
distractors.C: STORAGE_DAILY_HISTORY reports average daily bytes, not currency.

questions.scenario: A clone group consists of tables T1 (original), T2 (clone of T1), and T3 (clone of T2). T2 shares micro-partitions with T3. An administrator drops T2.
questions.stem: When does ownership of the shared micro-partitions transfer from T2 to T3?

options.text: Immediately when T2 is dropped
When the micro-partitions exit Time Travel and would otherwise enter Fail-safe
After the Fail-safe period for T2 expires
Only when T3 is explicitly altered to claim ownership

explanation.correct: When a table in a clone group is dropped, ownership of shared micro-partitions is transferred to the next table in the clone group when the micro-partitions exit Time Travel and would otherwise enter Fail-safe.

distractors.A: Transfer does not happen immediately at drop; the Time Travel period must expire first.
distractors.C: Transfer happens before Fail-safe, not after it expires.
distractors.D: Transfer is automatic; no explicit ALTER TABLE is needed.

questions.scenario: An organization wants to manage costs for a large 200 GB high-churn dimension table that gets updated 20 times daily.
questions.stem: Which TWO strategies reduce CDP storage costs for this table? (Select TWO)

options.text: Create the table as transient with DATA_RETENTION_TIME_IN_DAYS=0
Increase the warehouse size used to query the table
Periodically copy the transient table into a permanent table as a backup
Enable automatic clustering on the table
Set FAIL_SAFE_DAYS=0 on the permanent table

explanation.correct: For large high-churn tables, the recommended strategy is to create them as transient with zero Time Travel and periodically copy them into a permanent table for backup protection.

distractors.B: Warehouse size affects query performance, not storage costs.
distractors.D: Automatic clustering affects query performance through data organization, not CDP storage costs.
distractors.E: FAIL_SAFE_DAYS is not a configurable parameter; Fail-safe is always 7 days for permanent tables.

questions.scenario: An administrator views a cloned table's size in Snowsight and sees it reports 100 GB.
questions.stem: Why might this displayed size NOT reflect the actual physical storage the table contributes to the account?

options.text: Snowsight always underreports storage by approximately 10%
The displayed size shows active bytes, but a cloned table shares micro-partitions and may contribute less actual physical storage
Compression ratios are not factored into the displayed size
The display excludes data in external stages referenced by the table

explanation.correct: The size displayed represents active bytes. For cloned tables, the actual physical storage contribution is less because the clone shares micro-partitions with the original table until modifications are made.

distractors.A: Snowsight does not systematically underreport by a percentage.
distractors.C: The displayed size already accounts for compressed storage.
distractors.D: External stage data is not part of table size reporting.

questions.scenario: A team deletes 50% of the rows in a permanent table. They check the table size in Snowsight immediately after.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about storage for tables with deleted data are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: The displayed table size in Snowsight includes Time Travel and Fail-safe bytes
Deleted data is maintained through Time Travel and Fail-safe, incurring storage costs beyond the displayed table size
Storage is charged for data in Active, Time Travel, and Fail-safe states sequentially
Deleted data is immediately removed from all storage once the DELETE statement commits
Only the most recent deletion is retained in Time Travel

explanation.correct: Deleted data incurs storage through Time Travel and Fail-safe beyond what the displayed size shows, and storage is charged for data regardless of whether it is in Active, Time Travel, or Fail-safe state — these states are sequential.

distractors.A: The displayed size shows only active bytes; Time Travel and Fail-safe bytes are NOT included.
distractors.D: Deleted data is NOT immediately removed; it transitions through TT and Fail-safe.
distractors.E: All deletions within the retention period are maintained, not just the most recent.

questions.scenario: A Snowflake administrator wants to monitor storage across their entire account using Snowsight.
questions.stem: Which TWO categories can they filter storage by in the Consumption page? (Select TWO)

options.text: By Region (US, EU, APAC)
By Type (Database, Fail Safe, Stage)
By Object (specific database or stage)
By User (who created the data)
By Compression Ratio

explanation.correct: The storage history bar graph in Snowsight can be filtered By Type (Database, Fail Safe, Stage) or By Object (specific databases or stages).

distractors.A: Region-based filtering is not available on the storage consumption page.
distractors.D: User-based filtering is not available for storage views.
distractors.E: Compression ratio is not a filter option.

questions.scenario: A team migrates data from permanent tables to transient tables to reduce storage costs.
questions.stem: What is the correct sequence of steps for this migration?

options.text: DROP the permanent table, then CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE with the same name
ALTER TABLE to change the table type from permanent to transient
CLONE the permanent table as transient, then DROP the original
CREATE TRANSIENT TABLE ... AS SELECT from the permanent table, apply privileges, DROP the original, then optionally rename

explanation.correct: The migration process is: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT to populate the transient table, apply access control privileges, DROP the original permanent table, then optionally rename the new table.

distractors.A: Dropping first would lose the data before creating the replacement.
distractors.B: ALTER TABLE cannot change a table from permanent to transient.
distractors.C: Cloning preserves the table type; you cannot clone a permanent table into a transient one directly.

questions.scenario: A Snowflake account on Standard Edition has a permanent table with Time Travel enabled.
questions.stem: What is the maximum Time Travel retention period available for this table?

options.text: 0 or 1 day
Up to 7 days
Up to 30 days
Up to 90 days

explanation.correct: On Standard Edition, permanent tables can have a Time Travel retention period of 0 or 1 day only. Extended Time Travel (up to 90 days) requires Enterprise Edition.

distractors.B: 7 days is the Fail-safe period, not the maximum Time Travel retention on Standard Edition.
distractors.C: 30 days is available only on Enterprise Edition or higher.
distractors.D: 90 days is the maximum on Enterprise Edition, not Standard.

questions.scenario: A team wants to understand the cost components associated with Snowflake backups.
questions.stem: Which THREE cost components are associated with backups? (Select THREE)

options.text: Network transfer fees for backup replication
Restore compute using Snowflake-managed warehouses
Backup storage for retained backup data
Backup compute for scheduled backup creation and expiration
Backup licensing fees per table
Backup verification compute for integrity checks

explanation.correct: Backup costs include: backup compute (scheduled creation/expiration), restore compute (Snowflake-managed warehouses for restoring), and backup storage (cloud object storage for backup data).

distractors.A: Network transfer fees for backups are not listed as a separate backup cost component.
distractors.E: There are no per-table licensing fees for backups.
distractors.F: Backup verification compute is not a documented cost component.

questions.scenario: An administrator creates a temporary table for an ETL process. The session remains active for 6 hours before terminating.
questions.stem: What is the maximum CDP storage charge incurred for data in this temporary table?

options.text: 8 days (1 day Time Travel + 7 days Fail-safe)
7 days (Fail-safe only)
1 day (Time Travel only, no Fail-safe)
0 days (temporary tables incur no CDP charges)

explanation.correct: Temporary tables have a maximum of 1 day Time Travel and 0 days Fail-safe. The Time Travel period ends when the table is dropped or the session ends, so the maximum CDP charge is 1 day.

distractors.A: 8 days applies to permanent tables (1 day TT + 7 days Fail-safe on Standard Edition), not temporary tables.
distractors.B: Temporary tables have no Fail-safe period.
distractors.D: Temporary tables can incur up to 1 day of Time Travel storage charges.

questions.scenario: A dropped column still appears to consume storage when an administrator checks the physical bytes for a table.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about storage after dropping a column are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: The physical bytes for the dropped column data remain in storage
The dropped column data is immediately deleted from all micro-partitions
The displayed table size may be larger than what a full table scan would read
Dropped columns are moved to a separate archive table
Dropping a column triggers an automatic table rebuild

explanation.correct: Dropping a column does not immediately delete the physical bytes. The data remains in storage, and the displayed table size may be larger than the bytes actually scanned in a query since the dropped column's data still exists physically.

distractors.B: The data is NOT immediately deleted; physical bytes persist in existing micro-partitions.
distractors.D: There is no separate archive table for dropped column data.
distractors.E: Dropping a column does not trigger an automatic rebuild of the table.
